newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia unions start countdown to Feb. 11 strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombia unions start countdown to Feb. 11 strike.

text.p: Colombia's public sector unions rejected further talks with the government Sunday and launched the countdown to a national strike due to start on Feb. 11, union officials said.

Union leaders accused the government of "deceipt and trickery" in negotiations which broke down in the early hours Sunday. The union chiefs voted not to return to talks after a closed-doors meeting among themselves which ended early Sunday afternoon.

About 800,000 state employees across the country are expected to back the strike, which labor analysts predict will paralyze key economic and social sectors including oil, telecommunications, education, health and transport.

"In the light of the lack of respect shown by the government, legal action being undertaken against some of our members and claims that the guerrilla is infiltrating the strike, we believe the authorities are trying to undermine the labor movement," said Wilson Borja, head of the main state workers'union FENALTRASE.
"There is no possibility of returning to the negotiating table and we will spend the rest of today and Monday laying out final plans for the strike," he added.

The workers are protesting a weighted 13.5 percent pay hike, below the 1996 inflation rate of 21.63 percent, what they fear are government plans for the creeping privatization of state-owned industries and the gradual whittling away of labor rights.
At least 14 union members of the state phone company Telecom face legal action for a strike which shut down phone services for eight days in 1992 after the government declared it illegal.

In addition, 14 members of the main oil workers' union USO have either been convicted or are awaiting trial accused of sabotaging key oil infrastructure and of links to the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest leftist guerrilla force.
Union leaders say the men were arrested on trumped-up charges in a bid to undermine labor solidarity.

The government and the armed forces, meanwhile, launched emergency security measures over the weekend designed to prevent a wave of guerrilla attacks which they say are being timed to coincide with the strike.
Borja said the claims of guerrilla infiltration were a means of justifying a crackdown on a "legitimate" labor protest and said he feared the security forces would use violence against demonstrators.
